contrasts.label: Bol or boule?
contrasts.description: Listen to the vowel between the consonants. These pairs contrast open-mid /ɔ/ with close /u/, both rounded vowels. This is separate from the /o–u/ lesson.

l1Notes.note: Avoid substituting an English vowel-plus-r sequence for the vowel followed by the French rhotic in cor/cour and sort/sourd.
French /ɔ/ here is the open-mid category, distinct from the close-mid /o/ taught in another lesson.

contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French, in isolated one-syllable words without a final schwa. Final /ʁ/ may lengthen the preceding vowel; the broad transcription omits that contextual length in both members. Keep /ɔ/ distinct from /o/ and /u/ distinct from /y/. Sourd uses its masculine form, with no pronounced final d.

contrasts.label: Pur or peur?
contrasts.description: Both target vowels are front and rounded: close /y/ versus open-mid /œ/. Listen to the vowel before the final French r. The separate /y–ø/ lesson uses a different mid vowel.

l1Notes.note: French /y/ is one rounded vowel, not the English sequence in you. Compare the complete vowel quality before r.
Both targets require front rounded vowel categories; do not substitute ordinary Spanish /u/ or /e/.

pairs.note: Bure is a real but less-frequent noun for coarse woollen cloth; use the first TLFi sense.

contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French citation forms. Every pair has a medial target followed by /ʁ/. Contextual vowel length is omitted symmetrically in broad IPA; no /œ–ø/ merger is made. Sur is the fully pronounced isolated preposition, not a reduced conversational form. Bure is a less-frequent cloth word, included as a real lexical item rather than a fabricated form.

words.meaning: a full-width strip of fabric or wallpaper

pairs.note: Lé names a strip of fabric or wallpaper. Retain the accent: this noun /le/ is distinct from the article le /lə/.

contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French in isolation. Lit, nid, nez and prix have no final spoken t, d, z or x in these forms. Lé is a noun meaning a strip of fabric or wallpaper, not the article le /lə/; retain its written accent in any synthesis request. Prix/pré have a two-consonant onset but the same final-vowel target position.
